name: Ku Waru
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_locator: Section 3 'Aspects of Ku Waru segmental phonology and prosody', pp. 43-44 (extract pp. 5-6; page headed '..ordinary means 43' below Table 1, running onto '44 Alan Rumsey'); fn. 8 p. 43 (monosyllables, naá vs na); p. 46 (extract p. 8) for 'nor is any role played by a distinction of that kind among syllables within words.. the Ku Waru tone system' Same statement in Rumsey 2007, Anthropological Linguistics 49: 237-238, fn. 4-5 pp. 272-273.
catalog_quote: In Ku Waru, all polysyllabic words when pronounced carefully in isolation have within them a single syllable with a pitch peak which is higher than that of any other syllable within the word; for about 80% of them it is the final syllable. All monosyllabic words also have a pitch peak which is of about the same level as that of the high-toned syllable in polysyllabic words. In the practical orthography which is used here, for polysyllabic words, high pitch, if shown at all, is shown (with an acute accent mark ΄) only when it falls on a non-final syllable. All other polysyllabic words have the default pitch peak on the final syllable. Examples of words with contrasting pitch patterns are: koma ‘carry on one’s shoulder’ / kóma ‘wet’; toba hit:FUT.3s / tóba hit:NF.3s ... Unlike in English and other languages with stress-accent systems, the syllables with pitch peaks in Ku Waru are not, ipso facto, longer or of higher energy level than others. Regardless of pitch level, word-final syllables, especially in connected speech (as opposed to elicited single words) tend to be shorter than initial and medial ones. Indeed, when final syllables are open (i.e. vowel final) ones with high vowels, in connected speech the vowel is often omitted altogether, leaving the word with no high-toned syllable. In such cases, the underlying presence of a final high-toned syllable is signalled by the absence of any high-toned syllable elsewhere in the word (cf. Merlan and Rumsey 1991:324).
world_status: statement found in an open source

All monosyllabic words also have a pitch peak which is of about the same level as that of the high-toned syllable in polysyllabic words.[fn…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prosody is a culminative high-pitch (tone / 'pitch accent') system, not stress: each word has exactly one high-pitched syllable; by default (about 80% of words) it is the word-final syllable, but its position is lexically and grammatically contrastive (kóma vs koma, tóba vs toba), so non-final accent must be marked. The accented syllable carries no extra length or intensity; word-final syllables are in fact the shortest and a final high vowel may drop in connected speech, the word's final accent then being signalled only by the absence of high pitch elsewhere. Merlan & Rumsey 1991:324 labelled this 'pitch accent'; Rumsey 2007/2010 prefers to call it a (restricted) tone system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the system is stated to assign a pitch peak to just one syllable per word, and no strong/weak distinction among other syllables plays any role (Rumsey 2010: 47).
new_statements.exceptions: ~20% of polysyllabic words have the peak on a non-final syllable (lexically specified, marked with acute in the orthography); a handful of monosyllables with phonetically long (bimoraic) vowels, e.g. naá 'not' vs na 'I', carry the high tone on the second mora; in connected speech a final open high-vowel syllable may be elided, leaving no surface high-toned syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about words 'pronounced carefully in isolation' (citation forms); Rumsey notes final-syllable shortening/elision in connected speech and that the sung tom yaya melody largely overrides lexical tone. Described variety is the Ku Waru dialect of Bo-Ung.
new_statements.identity_note: All accessible descriptions are of Ku Waru ('Steep Stone'), the westernmost dialect area of Bo-Ung/Mbo-Ung [mux], straddling the Tambul Range on the western edge of the Nebilyer Valley (Rumsey 2010: 39). Glottolog 5.1 attaches Merlan & Rumsey 1991 (Ku Waru) to boun1245 but lists only Mara-Gomu (mara1405) and Miyemu (miye1238) as dialect nodes; Ku Waru has no separate glottocode. Rumsey explicitly rejects a stress analysis: the system is culminative lexical high pitch (default word-final), labelled 'pitch accent' in Merlan & Rumsey 1991 and 'tone' in Rumsey 2007/2010 -- catalog entry should be coded pitch accent/tonal rather than fixed: final syllable stress.

new_statements.quote: Ku Waru can best be described as having a pitch accent system, like Japanese. [...] But we would not describe Ku Waru as a ‘tone language’, for (summarily-stated), unlike in true ‘tone languages’ such as Chinese, pitch in Ku Waru is not contrastive at the level of the syllable or mora, but at the level of the word. [...] First, there is a general regularity in the position of the pitch peak: in a very high proportion of words, it occurs on the final syllable. And second, pitch accent has a very low functional yield: there are few pairs like the one illustrated above, in which the difference between two words consists only in a difference in placement of the accent.

new_statements.relation_note: Same system as the catalog's Rumsey 2010 quote (one pitch peak per word, mostly on the final syllable) and same reading as the existing verified statement ('pitch accent'); adds the explicit word-level (not syllable/mora) domain, the final-syllable default, the low functional yield, the lápa/lapá minimal pair and the accent-transfer-under-i-loss rule. It disputes only the TYPE LABEL: the catalog record's kind is 'tonal', whereas Merlan & Rumsey 1991 say 'we would not describe Ku Waru as a tone language' and call it pitch accent 'like Japanese' (Rumsey 2007 fn.4 notes this earlier label himself).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ku Waru has a word-level pitch accent (explicitly 'not a tone language'): each word has one pitch peak whose position is contrastive but largely predictable, falling on the final syllable in 'a very high proportion of words'; pitch is independent of vowel length and loudness, so that pairs like lápa 'father' vs lapá 'feather headdress' differ only in the position of the pitch peak while both sound initially 'stressed' to an English ear; functional load of accent placement is very low; in the verb paradigms accent is marked only when it is NOT on the final syllable. End of B.2 adds: when an accented word-final i loses syllabicity after a non-stop consonant, the accent (pitch rise) transfers to that consonant (pengí 'head').
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned; the authors treat perceived 'stress' (energy level) as separate from and non-contrastive beside the pitch accent, and give no secondary-accent rule
new_statements.exceptions: a minority of words have a non-final pitch peak (e.g. lápa 'father'; certain verb forms, marked in the paradigms only when non-final); accented final high vowel i may be desyllabified with the pitch rise transferred to the preceding non-occlusive consonant
new_statements.identity_note: The 1991 sketch (Appendix B) describes Bo Ung, Ku Waru dialect, as spoken at Kailge in the western Nebilyer Valley (Western Highlands Province, PNG), part of the Hagen-Kaugel (Melpa/Mbo-Ung) dialect continuum; same variety as Rumsey 2007/2010.

No word-stress placement rule stated.

sources.citation: Rumsey, Alan. 2007. Musical, poetic, and linguistic form in Tom Yaya sung narratives from Papua New Guinea. Anthropological Linguistics 49(3/4): 235-282.
sources.note: pp. 237-238: same statement as 2010 (single pitch-peak syllable per word, ~80% word-final, contrastive pairs koma/kóma, toba/tóba; unlike stress-accent languages the peak syllable is not longer or higher-energy). Fn. 4 (p. 272): Merlan & Rumsey 1991:324 called this a 'pitch accent' system; following Hyman 2006 Rumsey now avoids that label and speaks of the Ku Waru tone system. Fn. 5: monosyllables all have the same early-peak falling pattern except a few bimoraic words (naá 'not').
